subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does GNI per capita measure?
options: The total value of exports divided by the number of workers
The Gross National Income of a country divided by its total population
The average wage of factory workers in a country
The value of goods produced only within a country's own borders
questions.explain: GNI per capita is a country's total income (including earnings from abroad) shared out per person, giving an average figure.

questions.q: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines which three measures?
options: Birth rate, death rate and migration rate
Life expectancy, education and income (GNI per capita)
Literacy, employment and industrial output
Health spending, food supply and clean water access
questions.explain: HDI is a composite index built from health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and income (GNI per capita).

questions.q: HDI values are expressed on a scale between which two numbers?
options: 0 and 1
1 and 10
0 and 100
questions.explain: HDI is scored from 0 (least developed) to 1 (most developed), with higher values showing greater human development.

questions.q: What does the infant mortality rate measure?
options: The number of deaths of children under one year old per 1000 live births per year
The number of live births per 1000 people per year
The average number of children born to each woman
The percentage of adults who can read and write
questions.explain: Infant mortality counts deaths of babies under one year per 1000 live births and is a sensitive indicator of a country's healthcare and development.

questions.q: Why is GNI per capita alone a limited measure of a country's development?
options: It cannot be calculated for large countries
It is an average that hides inequalities in how wealth is distributed
It only counts income earned by farmers
It changes too slowly to be useful
questions.explain: As a mean value, GNI per capita can conceal wide gaps between rich and poor within the same country.

questions.q: Why is HDI often regarded as a better measure of development than economic indicators alone?
options: It uses only the most recent income data
It combines social and economic factors to give a more rounded picture
It is easier and cheaper to calculate than GNI
It ignores misleading health statistics
questions.explain: By blending health, education and income, HDI captures quality of life as well as wealth.

questions.q: A country records a high GNI per capita but low life expectancy and low literacy. What does this most likely suggest?
options: The data must have been recorded incorrectly
Economic wealth is not being invested in health and education
The country has a very small population
The country has no natural resources
questions.explain: A gap between high income and poor social indicators suggests wealth is unevenly spread or not spent on public services.

questions.q: Why do many lower-income countries tend to have high birth rates?
options: Because governments legally require large families
Because children are needed for work and infant mortality is high, so families have more children
Because contraception is banned worldwide
Because life expectancy is very high
questions.explain: Where child labour supports families and many infants die young, people often have more children as security.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines a non-renewable resource?
options: A resource that is replaced naturally as fast as it is used
A finite resource that cannot be replaced within a human lifetime
A resource that can only be found in oceans
A resource that produces no pollution when used
questions.explain: Non-renewable resources such as coal, oil and gas are finite and take millions of years to form, so they cannot be replenished on a human timescale.

questions.q: Which group lists only fossil fuels?
options: Coal, oil and natural gas
Solar, wind and coal
Oil, uranium and hydroelectricity
Natural gas, wind and biomass
questions.explain: The three fossil fuels are coal, oil and natural gas, all formed from ancient organic matter.

questions.q: Why does resource consumption generally increase as a country becomes more developed?
options: Because populations always fall as countries develop
Because industrialisation and higher living standards raise demand for energy, water and goods
Because developed countries stop trading with others
Because resources become cheaper to ignore
questions.explain: Economic growth and rising incomes drive greater use of energy, water and manufactured products.

questions.q: A region is described as experiencing 'water stress'. What does this mean?
options: The water is too cold to use
The demand for water is greater than the available supply
The region only has salt water
The water is stored underground
questions.explain: Water stress occurs where demand exceeds the reliable supply, often due to high population, agriculture or low rainfall.

questions.q: A country has a rapidly growing population, expanding industry and a hot, dry climate. Which resource issue is it most likely to face?
options: A surplus of energy it cannot sell
Increasing pressure on water supplies and possible scarcity
A falling demand for food
No need to import any resources
questions.explain: Growing demand combined with low rainfall raises the risk of water scarcity in such regions.

questions.q: Which phrase best describes sustainable development?
options: Using as many resources as possible before they run out
Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Stopping all use of natural resources immediately
Developing only the wealthiest regions of a country
questions.explain: This is the widely used definition of sustainable development, balancing present needs against those of the future.

questions.q: Why is appropriate (intermediate) technology often more sustainable in lower-income communities?
options: It is the most expensive option available
It is small-scale, affordable and uses local skills and materials
It always relies on imported fossil fuels
It removes the need for any local labour
questions.explain: Appropriate technology suits local conditions, is low-cost and can be maintained by the community, making it sustainable.

questions.q: How does recycling help manage resources more sustainably?
options: It increases demand for new raw materials
It reduces demand for raw materials and cuts the amount of waste sent to landfill
It speeds up the use of fossil fuels
It has no effect on resource use
questions.explain: Reusing materials lowers the need to extract new resources and reduces waste, conserving resources for the future.

questions.q: A town wants to reduce its water consumption sustainably. Which strategy fits this aim best?
options: Encouraging households to leave taps running to keep pipes clean
Installing water meters and promoting water-saving devices to cut waste
Building larger reservoirs and using twice as much water
Banning the collection of rainwater
questions.explain: Metering and efficiency measures reduce demand and waste, making water use more sustainable.

questions.q: A community relies heavily on burning coal for energy. Which change would make its energy supply more sustainable?
options: Increasing coal imports from other countries
Switching some supply to renewable sources such as solar or wind
Closing all schools to save electricity
Using coal more quickly before it runs out
questions.explain: Renewables like solar and wind are replenished naturally and produce fewer emissions, making the supply more sustainable.
